newsitem.title: USA: Tiger Woods craze drives golf industry - executive.
newsitem.headline: Tiger Woods craze drives golf industry - executive.

text.p: Golf sensation Tiger Woods is driving young people to take up the sport and fuelling growth in the golf business, the chairman of a prominent chain of golf courses and driving ranges said.

"Ever since he became a pro, we've seen a 50 percent increase of young people taking classes at our junior clinics and they come from all ethnic backgrounds. It's phenomenal," said Family Golf Centres Inc. Chairman Dominic Chang.
Both boys and girls were showing up in droves for lessons, he said, a healthy sign for the future of the industry.
A new customer demographic has emerged, which he termed '3-setters', meaning young people who buy three sets of golf clubs over a period of just a few years.

"They get their first set in early adolescence when they start and after two or three years they buy another set as teenagers. Then in high school and college, they will want an even better set ... It's a phenemom we intend to cultivate," Chang said on a conference call after the company reported a nearly fivefold increase in annual profits on Friday.

He said Family Golf was also seeing far more women sign up for lessons and a broader surge in demand for lessons. Individual half hour lessons at the company's four New York state facilities grew 53 percent last year, he said.
Chang also said the company was in negotiations for an acquisition in New York City but he did not disclose details, saying the company did not yet have all the approvals in hand.
Tiger Woods, 21, was three times the U.S. amateur champion before he dropped out of Stanford University to become a professional golfer.

He immediately landed a $60 million pact with Nike and won two PGA Tour events -- the Las Vegas Invitational and Walt Disney World Classic -- in one of the most impressive debuts in professional golf history.
Family Golf earned $5.2 million, or 51 cents a share, compared with nearly $1.1 million, or 20 cents a share, in 1995. Sales more than doubled to $27.9 million.
